content.overview: Git's functionality can be extended through custom commands, aliases, and extensions. This module covers how to create your own Git commands to automate common workflows, customize Git's behavior, and integrate with external tools.

steps.title: Understanding Git's Extensibility
steps.content: Git is designed to be extensible, allowing users to create custom commands and workflows. There are several ways to extend Git's functionality, from simple aliases to full-fledged extensions.

steps.title: Creating Git Aliases
steps.content: Git aliases are shortcuts for longer Git commands. They can save time and make complex commands easier to remember.

behindTheCommand.title: Alias Storage and Scope
behindTheCommand.content:
Git aliases are stored in Git's configuration files:

1. **System-wide**: `/etc/gitconfig` - affects all users on the system
2. **Global**: `~/.gitconfig` or `~/.config/git/config` - affects all your repositories
3. **Local**: `.git/config` in a repository - affects only that repository

Aliases can be simple command substitutions or complex shell commands. For shell commands, prefix with an exclamation point (!).

steps.title: Advanced Git Aliases
steps.content: Advanced Git aliases can include shell commands, parameters, and even call other Git commands. These powerful aliases can automate complex workflows.

fileChanges.description: Create a reference file with useful Git aliases
fileChanges.content:
# Useful Git Aliases

## Basic Aliases

```bash
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.ci commit
git config --global alias.st status
```

## Workflow Aliases

```bash
# Unstage files
git config --global alias.unstage 'reset HEAD --'

# Show the last commit
git config --global alias.last 'log -1 HEAD'

# Amend the last commit
git config --global alias.amend 'commit --amend'

# Undo the last commit (keeping changes)
git config --global alias.undo 'reset --soft HEAD~1'

# Show a pretty commit log
git config --global alias.lg "log --color --graph --pretty=format:'%Cred%h%Creset -%C(yellow)%d%Creset %s %Cgreen(%cr) %C(bold blue)<%an>%Creset' --abbrev-commit"
```

## Advanced Aliases

```bash
# Show all branches, including remote branches
git config --global alias.branches 'branch -a'

# Show all tags
git config --global alias.tags 'tag -l'

# Show all remotes
git config --global alias.remotes 'remote -v'

# Show a summary of incoming/outgoing commits
git config --global alias.incoming '!git remote update -p; git log ..@{u}'
git config --global alias.outgoing 'log @{u}..'

# Clean up local branches that have been merged
git config --global alias.cleanup "!git branch --merged | grep -v '\*\|master\|main\|develop' | xargs -n 1 git branch -d"

# Create a new branch and switch to it
git config --global alias.nb '!f() { git checkout -b "$1"; }; f'

# Save work in progress
git config --global alias.wip '!git add -A && git commit -m "WIP"'
git config --global alias.unwip '!git log -n 1 | grep -q -c "WIP" && git reset HEAD~1'
```

## Using Aliases

Once configured, you can use aliases like this:

```bash
# Instead of git checkout
git co main

# Instead of git status
git st

# Show a pretty log graph
git lg

# Create and switch to a new branch
git nb feature/new-feature

# Save work in progress
git wip

# Resume work after WIP
git unwip
```

behindTheCommand.title: Shell Command Aliases
behindTheCommand.content:
For more complex aliases that use shell commands:

1. **Use the exclamation point (!)** to indicate a shell command
2. **Access parameters** with $1, $2, etc. (or use a shell function)
3. **Chain commands** with && or |
4. **Use quotes** to handle spaces and special characters

Shell command aliases can be powerful but may not be portable across different operating systems.

steps.title: Creating Git Extensions
steps.content: Git extensions are custom commands that extend Git's functionality. They can be written in any language and are invoked as 'git-command'.

commands.command:
cat > ~/bin/git-hello << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello, Git extension world!"
EOF

fileChanges.description: Create a more useful Git extension
fileChanges.content:
#!/bin/bash

# git-summary - Show a summary of the current repository

# Ensure we're in a git repository
if ! git rev-parse --git-dir > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Error: Not a git repository"
  exit 1
fi

# Get repository name
repo_name=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")

# Get current branch
current_branch=$(git symbolic-ref --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo "detached HEAD")

# Get commit count
commit_count=$(git rev-list --count HEAD)

# Get contributor count
contributor_count=$(git shortlog -s | wc -l)

# Get file count
file_count=$(git ls-files | wc -l)

# Get repository size
repo_size=$(du -sh . | awk '{print $1}')

# Get last commit date
last_commit_date=$(git log -1 --format=%cd --date=relative)

# Print summary
echo "Repository Summary: $repo_name"
echo "----------------------------"
echo "Current branch: $current_branch"
echo "Commit count: $commit_count"
echo "Contributors: $contributor_count"
echo "Files: $file_count"
echo "Repository size: $repo_size"
echo "Last commit: $last_commit_date"
echo ""

# Show branch status
echo "Branch Status:"
git branch -v
echo ""

# Show recent commits
echo "Recent Commits:"
git log --oneline -n 5

behindTheCommand.title: How Git Extensions Work
behindTheCommand.content:
Git extensions work through a simple naming convention:

1. **Create an executable file** named `git-command`
2. **Place it in your PATH** (e.g., ~/bin/ or /usr/local/bin/)
3. **Make it executable** with `chmod +x git-command`

When you run `git command`, Git looks for an executable named `git-command` in your PATH. This allows you to extend Git with commands written in any language.

steps.title: Sharing and Managing Custom Commands
steps.content: Custom Git commands and configurations can be shared across teams and projects. This ensures consistent workflows and tooling.

commands.command:
cat > .gitconfig.shared << 'EOF'
[alias]
  st = status
  co = checkout
  br = branch
  ci = commit
  lg = log --graph --pretty=format:'%Cred%h%Creset -%C(yellow)%d%Creset %s %Cgreen(%cr) %C(bold blue)<%an>%Creset' --abbrev-commit
[core]
  editor = code --wait
  autocrlf = input
[pull]
  rebase = true
EOF

behindTheCommand.title: Team Standardization Approaches
behindTheCommand.content:
There are several approaches to standardizing Git commands across a team:

1. **Shared configuration files**: Use `include.path` to include team-wide configurations
2. **Project-specific scripts**: Include scripts in the repository that everyone can use
3. **Custom packages**: Create installable packages with your team's Git extensions
4. **Documentation**: Maintain documentation of recommended aliases and workflows

Standardizing Git commands helps ensure consistent workflows and reduces friction when collaborating.
